headline: Assemble a verification verdict out of component results through the operation the package captured at load, and refuse the reserved end-of-contents encoding where an element belongs.
summary: A verdict built from several component checks is worth only what the operation awaiting those components is worth. `Promise.all` builds its promise from the receiver it is called on, so reading the global binding at the call site hands that construction to whatever the binding holds, and a replacement that resolves an array without awaiting anything supplies its own values to the caller as the verdict. That reached the proof-of-possession verifier, the composite signature arm, WebAuthn attestation, and the CMC verifier. Every aggregation and every refusal in those paths now goes through operations taken when the module loads. A caller on an unmodified runtime sees no behavioral change and no emitted bytes change. Separately, the strict decoder accepted universal tag 0 as an element, which X.690 reserves for the end-of-contents pair that DER does not permit at all.

Fixed: `pki.crmf.verifyPop` assembled its verdict from the per-message results with `Promise.all` read from the global binding at the call. `Promise.all` builds its promise from its receiver, so a replacement whose `all` resolves an array without awaiting the component verifications hands its own values back as the verdict, and an unverified proof of possession was reported `verified: true`. The composite signature arm failed the same way: its verdict is `ok` only when both the ML-DSA and the traditional component resolve true, so an `all` resolving `[true, true]` reported a signature whose halves were never checked as verified, reachable through `pki.cms.verify` and `pki.path.validate` wherever a composite algorithm is in use. The same shape decided more than the aggregations. `pki.webauthn.verify` returned its refusals as rejected promises and folded its attestation trust-path checks over a seed built the same way, so a replacement whose `reject` resolves turned an unsupported attestation format, an attestation missing its attested credential data, and a failed policy check into a pass, while one settling the seed without awaiting the chain produced a verdict for a path that was never walked. `pki.cmc` gated its verify body on one of these and returned its refusals through another. `pki.ocsp.buildRequest` and `pki.ocsp.sign` awaited the pair of CertID hashes that bind a response to the certificate it answers for, and `pki.cms.sign` awaited each signer's digest and signature, so a replacement settling early emitted a structure whose SignerInfos were never completed. `pki.kem.encapsulate` and `pki.kem.decapsulate`, the composite ML-KEM pair, settled their two component results through `Promise.allSettled` before either shared secret was used or wiped, so a replacement reporting both components fulfilled with values of its own handed the combiner material it chose and skipped the wipe of the real secrets, which is the hybrid's whole premise that one broken component does not open the message. Each component refusal there was returned as a rejected promise too, so a `kem/bad-key` or `kem/decapsulation-failed` verdict could be turned into a pass. The `pki.acme` and `pki.est` clients gated each verb's body on one of these and returned their refusals through another, so a replacement could let a verb run against a refused request or turn an enrollment refusal into a pass, and the HTTP transport under all of them did the same, including `peerChain`'s refusal to tunnel through a proxy. The certificate-transparency log fetch was gated the same way. The transport also constructed the promise wrapping each request with `new Promise` off the global binding, which is the widest of these: a replacement need not run the executor at all and can settle with a value of its own, so every revocation, enrollment, directory and log response a caller awaited could be one nobody fetched. Both request paths and the backoff timer now construct through the captured constructor, the spelling the crypto engine and the async guard already used. All of these now call operations captured when the module loads, as the signing verbs already did for their own self-checks, and no module that takes those captures reads a replaceable promise operation at call time any more. Nothing about the emitted encodings changes, and OpenSSL validates the same bytes as before.

`pki.asn1.decode` accepted universal tag 0 as an element, and every parser built on it did the same. X.690 section 8.1.5 defines that tag only as the first octet of the two-octet end-of-contents pair that closes an indefinite-length encoding, which DER does not permit, so no DER element carries it. A `00 00` pair where a member was expected decoded as an empty element of universal type 0 and was passed on to whatever read that position. The decoder now refuses it at the tag-length-value boundary with `asn1/reserved-tag`, under both the strict and the BER-tolerant read, and every format parser inherits that. A context-class or application-class tag number 0 is untouched, so `[0]` members are unaffected. The long-form tag indicator `0x1F` is untouched as well: `1F 1F` still reads as universal tag 31. The long-form spelling of tag number 0, `1F 00`, draws `asn1/non-minimal-tag` instead, because a tag number below 31 has to use the short form. `pki.inspect.asn1` continues to render a refused file as a header walk, and names the refusal that produced it.
